record.title: Ask Which, Not How Good: Sizing Benchmarks Scored by an LLM
record.summary: A measurement study of 373,019 LLM judgments reports a hard limit on the resolution of single-judge pointwise benchmarks: increasing item count cannot remove system-by-judge variance. Pairwise scoring reduces that variance in the tested setup but introduces an 8.6-point presentation-order effect. Across the studied benchmarks, measured 95% floors of 0.41–1.24 points exceeded the median reported gain of 0.28 points; all 17 recovered MT-Bench gains in the matched comparison fell below that benchmark’s measured floor. These are author-reported findings, not an independent replication.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across 373,019 judgments, the author reports that single-judge pointwise scoring has an item-count ceiling imposed by system-by-judge variance, while paired preference scoring reduces that variance but retains order bias: the same system wins 8.6 percentage points more often when presented first. Measured 95% floors were 0.41–1.24 points on a 0–5 scale, above a median reported improvement of 0.28 points. On the one repeatedly studied benchmark with an exact match, all 17 recovered MT-Bench improvements fell below its measured floor.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The reported floors and biases are author-reported and depend on the tested system panels, judges, rubrics and benchmark sets. They do not establish that every LLM-judged benchmark is unresolved or that pairwise evaluation with one judge is generally adequate.

evidence_gaps.description: Independent replication of variance decomposition, benchmark floors and order-bias estimates on current judges and additional benchmark families is absent.

brief.importance_rationale: If the findings generalize, they show that many small LLM-judge benchmark gains cannot be resolved by simply adding more items, and that pairwise comparisons exchange one measurement problem for order bias. This could materially change benchmark design and claims; the evidence comes from the paper’s tested judges, systems and benchmark sets.
limitations: Results are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced.
The system panels vary across some benchmark sets, limiting unconditional cross-set comparisons.
Single-judge ceiling results concern pointwise rubric scoring; paired preference scoring changes the measurement problem but introduces presentation-order bias.
Several conclusions are based on a limited number of systems or item sets; transfer to all LLM-judged evaluations is not established.

technical.claimed_result: Across 373,019 judgments, the author reports that single-judge pointwise scoring has an item-count ceiling imposed by system-by-judge variance, while paired preference scoring reduces that variance but retains order bias: the same system wins 8.6 percentage points more often when presented first. Measured 95% floors were 0.41–1.24 points on a 0–5 scale, above a median reported improvement of 0.28 points. technical.compute_or_cost: No compute-cost comparison is central to the result.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper reports a variance decomposition, measured benchmark resolution floors, pairwise order bias and an audit of reporting practices; these remain author-reported.
technical.implementation_status: Research analysis; no evaluation standard or policy adoption is claimed.
technical.mechanism: Generalizability-theory variance decomposition treats the system as the measurement object. Under pointwise scoring with one judge, system-by-judge variance imposes an asymptotic ceiling that more items cannot remove; pairwise preference changes the variance structure but can introduce order effects.
technical.regime: Analysis of pointwise judgments on MT-Bench, Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval 2, with 42 systems, nine judges and three replicates; the screened set adds paired null comparisons. Pairwise order-effect analyses and a survey audit use separate samples described in the paper.
technical.reproducibility: Paper describes the design and model; independent analysis or replication was not performed in this review.
technical.strongest_baseline: Matched benchmark item sets, judges, rubric and scale across tested systems, with three repeated judgments; pairwise comparisons are presented in both orders.
